sections.h2: Smoke and CO affidavit before closing
sections.html:
Abington Township requires an affidavit at or before settlement on any single-family, two-family or multifamily dwelling. The seller swears that the house shows a clear street address, has smoke detectors and has at least one carbon monoxide detector. Under Resolution 92-008, a deed is not accepted for registration unless the certification comes with it.

Ordinance 1894 spells out the standards, and a buyer's agent will check them.

Ordinance 1894 requirements for the affidavit
RequirementWhat the ordinance requires
Address numeralsAt least three inches high on the street side, visible from the center of the street
Smoke detectorsOne on each level and in each bedroom or sleeping area
Carbon monoxide detectorNo more than 40 feet from every sleeping area
Detector approvalUL rated and approved

Breaking the ordinance is a summary offense. The penalty is a fine of $1,000 at most, up to 30 days in jail, or both, and each day of a continuing violation is charged separately. The affidavit form is in the township's document center. Alarms are cheap, and putting them in before you list removes a common closing delay.

sections.h2: No resale use and occupancy permit
sections.html:
Abington has no use and occupancy permit for residential properties. That review, with a Fire Marshal inspection, applies to commercial properties, new businesses and business transfers.

A typical house sale here carries less municipal paperwork than a town with a resale inspection, and the detector affidavit is the main township step. Work done without a permit is a separate matter. If you finished a basement, built a deck or added a bathroom, ask the Code Enforcement Division before you list.

sections.h2: What to prepare on the house itself
sections.html:
Look at the house as a buyer's agent would. From the curb, check that the numbers are readable from the middle of the street. Inside, count every sleeping area and find a detector for each one. Test each unit and swap out any that look worn or carry no UL mark.

If a previous owner finished the basement or attic, locate the permit papers now. Even a cash buyer will ask, and handing them over early keeps the deal moving.

The 2026 tax sheet splits the real estate bill among the township, the Abington School District, a school referendum levy and Montgomery County with its community college. The school district rate is 39.8992 mills, by far the largest piece.

A township realty transfer tax of 1 percent is collected by Montgomery County, on top of the state's 1 percent. Ask your closing agent whether the school district adds a share on your deed. Pennsylvania exempts some transfers, such as property passing by will or intestate succession.

The township does not assess property. The Montgomery County Board of Assessments does, and the last countywide reassessment was in 1998. The township bill, which also covers sewer and refuse, is mailed in the first week of February for a January to December year. The school bill follows in the first week of July and runs July to June, so the closing agent will prorate each bill from its own start date.

Owners of a primary residence can apply for a homestead exclusion through the Montgomery County Board of Assessments. Applications must arrive by March 1 to reduce the school tax bill.

For questions about the township tax sheet, call the Abington tax office at 267-536-1024 on weekdays between 8 am and 4 pm. Buyers often ask for the latest bill, so have both the township and school copies handy when you list.

Abington is a first-class township in Montgomery County, a first-ring suburb of Philadelphia, with a mid 2025 population estimate of 58,656. Owners live in 77.3 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $391,800, middle-of-the-market rent is $1,493, and middle household income is $103,645. Neighborhoods include Willow Grove, Roslyn, Crestmont, Glenside, Rydal, North Hills and Meadowbrook.

Seven SEPTA stations on three regional rail lines serve the township, with a ride to Center City under half an hour. Mention the train access when you market the house. Most of the township has public water from Aqua Pennsylvania and public sewer maintained by the township. The Abington School District is a separate body from the township government. About 92.5 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is low, and a listing with defects or title questions takes more effort to place.

sections.h2: Which sale route fits an Abington house?
sections.html:
Three paths are open. Listing with an agent puts the house in front of the most buyers, at the price of staging, open houses and a wait while the buyer's bank and inspector do their work. Skipping the agent saves the commission, though you then handle every form yourself, from the detector affidavit to the deed.

Selling for cash to a direct buyer removes showings and repair work. People pick it for estate houses, rentals with tenants, homes with code problems or a hard move-out date. The offer is lower because the buyer takes on the repairs, so set it next to your likely net from a listing after commissions, fix-up costs and the months you would keep paying the mortgage and utilities.

Whichever path you take, the Abington requirements stay the same: detector affidavit, tax bills and a deed recorded with the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds.

1. Test or add detectors on each level and beside every bedroom, and check your house numerals from the street.
  2. Sign the affidavit and file it with your closing documents.
  3. Pull the newest township and school bills.
  4. Request a payoff statement if a loan is still open.
  5. Decide who has authority to sign when an owner has died or several people share title.
  6. At the settlement table you sign the deed, and it goes to the county to be recorded.

With cash there is no lender appraisal or underwriting step, so the timeline rests mainly on title work and when you can be out.

If the owner has died, work out who may sign for the estate before anything else. A deed cannot be recorded until title is clean, and passing a house through an estate carries no state transfer tax, though the sale after it does.

If renters live there, the lease controls your timetable. Showings and move-out dates follow its terms and Pennsylvania landlord and tenant law. A buyer who wants to keep the renters will ask to see the lease and the rent history. The detector rules apply to rentals sold in the township as well.

faqs.q: Does Abington require a smoke and carbon monoxide certification when I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. Ordinance 1894 requires smoke detectors on each level and in each bedroom, plus a carbon monoxide detector within 40 feet of every sleeping area, with a seller's affidavit at or before settlement.

faqs.q: Is there a residential use and occupancy permit in Abington?
faqs.a: No. That review applies to commercial buildings and business transfers, not to a house sale.
The 2026 tax sheet shows a 1 percent real estate transfer tax, collected by Montgomery County. The state adds its own 1 percent. Ask the closing agent whether any other local share applies.

faqs.q: Who assesses property in Abington Township?
faqs.a: The Montgomery County Board of Assessments, not the township. The last countywide reassessment was in 1998, and interim bills reflect changes such as additions or demolitions.

faqs.q: When must I apply for the homestead exclusion?
faqs.a: Applications must reach the Board of Assessments by March 1 to cut the school tax bill. A move or a change of title means applying again.
